extracted.intended_audience: readers and writers of epic poetry; literary critics; educated general readership (Spectator readers)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on assessing and composing characters (actors) in heroic/epic poetry, focusing on variety, novelty, probability, suitability to subject and audience, and the effects of moral character on an audience's pity and terror.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variety of Characters
rubrics_metrics.description: The multitude and variety of characters is a principal excellence in epic poetry (Homer excels in the Multitude and Variety of his Characters). Every deity and prince should act a part suitable to no other deity; princes are distinguished by their manners as well as their dominions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim to supply a wide range of distinct characters so the reader can recognize speaker/actor by speech and action alone. Avoid having many characters of the same stamp; variety gives the poem liveliness and interest (contrast Homer’s variety with Virgil's more uniform secondary characters).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinctness of Character by Speech and Action
rubrics_metrics.description: There is scarce a speech or action in the Iliad which the reader may not ascribe to the person that speaks or acts, without seeing his name at the head of it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compose speeches and actions so they reveal character; each character’s diction, manner, and deeds should be individually recognizable. This distinctness aids reader sympathy and comprehension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty of Characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Novelty in characters (introducing persons unlike common figures — e.g., very long-lived personages, offspring of deities) is an important merit; Homer introduced unusual beings that suited an heroic poem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduce fresh, surprising figures or relationships where appropriate to enrich the epic; novelty should be fitting to the poem’s subject and not gratuitous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suitability of Characters to the Nature of the Poem
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters must be adapted to the nature of an heroic poem (every god admitted acts a part suitable to no other deity; gods and superior natures should behave with dignity and condescension befitting them).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure each character’s role, speech, and actions are congruent with their ontological status and the poem’s tone (e.g., angels should speak and act with suitable dignity; buffoons appropriate only in certain places).

rubrics_metrics.name: Probability (Plausibility) of Characters and Actions
rubrics_metrics.description: There must be a measure of probability annexed to the actors in an epic; chimerical or unsubstantial beings (allegorical personages) may lack the requisite probability for heroic poetry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preserve plausibility even amid the marvelous: extraordinary or allegorical figures should be handled so they do not break the reader’s sense of probability; where probability is weak, other merits (allegory, invention) must sufficiently justify their inclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use and Limits of Allegorical/Chimerical Characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Milton introduced allegorical beings (Sin and Death) to enlarge the cast; while this enriches the allegory, such unsubstantial beings are not always proper actors in an epic because they may lack probability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allegory can atone for a restricted cast but should be used carefully; allegorical characters may suit mock-heroic works or certain episodes, yet their inclusion in a serious epic must be justified by artistic necessity and treated so as to maintain plausibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relation of Heroes to the Intended Readership
rubrics_metrics.description: Choosing heroes closely related to the people for whom the poem is written gives a peculiar beauty and engages national sympathy (Achilles was Greek; Æneas was founder of Rome).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When possible, select protagonists who resonate with the poem’s primary audience to secure stronger emotional investment; Milton’s subject (Adam and Eve) is praised because it renders the poem universally relevant to all readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complexity and Variety in Antagonists
rubrics_metrics.description: An antagonist who displays many wiles, stratagems, disguises and varied appearances (e.g., Satan) enriches the fable and delights the reader by frequent discoveries of his devices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop the antagonist with resourcefulness, changing tactics and guises to create intrigue and sustained interest; avoid a one-note villain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of Uniformity Among Secondary Characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Uniformity among secondary characters (many 'men of the same stamp and character' as in Virgil) is a defect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate minor characters in temperament, duty, and manner to prevent monotony; even slight distinguishing traits can prevent a cast from blending into sameness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral Complexity and the Effect on Pity and Terror
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristotle’s observation: a person of consummate virtue falling into misfortune raises pity but not terror; a virtuous person mixed with infirmities excites both pity and terror because of resemblance to ourselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For tragic or moving effect, present heroes with humane flaws or infirmities rather than absolute perfection; moral complexity increases audience identification and emotional impact. (Addison notes exceptions in certain epic contexts where representative perfection may be appropriate.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Character Parts Should Fit Their Proper Roles (e.g., Angels, Gods)
rubrics_metrics.description: In Milton the angels are diversified and distinguished by their proper parts; nothing ascribed to Uriel, Gabriel, Michael or Raphael is out of character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assign roles and behaviors that suit a character’s nature and rank; maintain internal consistency so each named supernatural or divine actor behaves in a manner appropriate to their supposed function and dignity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using Correspondence as Source Material for Periodical Essays
rubrics_metrics.description: Letters from correspondents show which papers are acceptable and furnish materials for new speculations; the editor may reform a letter’s hints into his own plans, change language or thought, and omit compliments so long as sense is preserved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For periodical production, use readers’ letters both to gauge audience taste and as seeds for original essays; adapt rather than reproduce, altering wording and omitting excessive flattering passages where necessary, and use subscriber or closing sections to lengthen pieces if needed.
